title: Ancient Trees in New Zealand: Cities to Explore
meta_description: New Zealand's oldest tree, the kauri Tane Mahuta, predates the country's colonial plantings by a thousand years. {places} places, {trees} trees.
intro: New Zealand's old trees split across two entirely different timescales. Deep in Waipoua Forest stands Tane Mahuta, the largest known kauri alive, estimated at somewhere between 1,250 and 2,500 years old, a single tree that predates New Zealand's human settlement by more than a thousand years and is protected today by a boardwalk that never lets a boot touch its roots. Everything else mapped here is comparatively young and imported. Christchurch's oldest surviving oak went into the ground in 1863 to mark a royal wedding, and outlived the 2011 earthquake that flattened the buildings around its neighbours in Cranmer and Latimer Squares. Auckland's coronation oaks, planted for Edward VII and George V, and its Moreton Bay figs brought over from Australia, are barely a century old beside the kauri: a colony's civic ceremonies and a forest's own patience running on entirely different clocks.
